LETTER TO THE EDITOR
Treatment of progressive encephalo-
myelitis with rigidity and myoclonic
jerks with rituximab: a case report
S. Saidha a, M. Elamin a, G. Mullins a,
E. Chaila a, V. J. Tormey b,
M. J. Hennessy a
Departments of aNeurology and
bImmunolgy, University College Hospital
Galway, Galway, Ireland
Correspondence: Dr Hennessy, Depart-
ment of Neurology, University College
Hospital Galway, Galway, Ireland (tel.:
091542341; fax: 091542364; e-mail:
Michael.hennessy@mailn.hse.ie).
Keywords: demyelinating diseases,
movement disorders, neuroendocrinology,
neuroimmunology, neuropharmacology
Received 4 November 2007
Accepted 31 December 2007
Introduction
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid-
ity and myoclonic jerks (PERM) is a rare
autoimmune disorder with poor prognosis
[1,2]. Autoimmune polyglandular syn-
dromes (APS) are rare endocrinopathies
characterized by the coexistence of
diﬀerent combinations of autoimmune
endocrine insuﬃciencies [3]. We report a
case of association between PERM and
APS and describe response to immuno-
modulatory therapy.
Case report
A 60-year-old female presented to the
neurology services with paraspinal muscle
rigidity, muscle spasms and new onset
scoliosis. Previous history included symp-
tomatic Hashimoto /C213s thyroiditis.
Although initial thyroid stimulating hor-
mone was elevated and free thyroxine
reduced, these remained stable with
thyroxine replacement.
At 62 years, she developed an ataxic
gait with dysmetria and deteriorating
mobility. Overtime oscillopsia developed
impaired reading and writing. By
65 years she was wheelchair bound. Type
1 diabetes mellitus was diagnosed fol-
lowing presentation with diabetic
ketoacidosis. Other complaints included
lower limb myoclonic jerks and
post-prandial abdominal cramps with
dyspepsia.
Neurological examination at presenta-
tion revealed paraspinal rigidity and
scoliosis with exaggerated lumbar
lordosis. Muscle power was normal with-
out fatigue. Reﬂexes were pathologically
brisk with extensor plantar responses.
Subsequent examinations revealed scan-
ning dysarthria, dysmetria and intention
tremor. Opsoclonus was prominent at rest
and in all directions of gaze.
Antiglutamic acid decarboxylase
(GAD) antibody was positive with a titre
of 87 U/ml (range 0–1 U/ml). Antinuclear
antibody was positive with a speckled
pattern (titre: 1/640). Antipancreatic islet
cell, anti-adrenal cortex, antitissue
transglutaminase and anti-endomysial
antibodies were positive. Antithyroid
peroxidase antibody was positive (titre:
>1000 U/ml). Duodenal biopsy demon-
strated villous atrophy. Cortisol levels,
pre- and post-synacthen were normal on
repeated sampling. Adrenocorticotrophic
hormone levels were normal.
Cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) analysis
demonstrated an elevated protein of
0.77 g/l (range 0.15–0.45 g/l), white cells
of 6/cmm (range 0–5/cmm) and normal
glucose. CSF oligoclonal bands were
absent. MRI of brain and spine and CT of
thorax, abdomen and pelvis were normal.
Muscle rigidity/spasms were well
controlled with benzodiazepines. Coeliac
disease was treated by a gluten free diet.
Speciﬁc immune treatment including
oral steroids, intravenous (IV) methyl-
prednisolone, methotrexate, azathioprine,
mycophenolate mofetil, IV immunoglob-
ulin, inﬂiximab (six infusions) and plasma
exchange were ineﬀective. Six cycles of the
B cell depleting antibody rituximab were
administered (dose: 375 mg/m
2). B cell
depletion was conﬁrmed by a CD19 count

of 0.001 · 109/l. Subsequently cerebellar
symptoms improved restoring ability to
eat using a fork and knife. Dysarthria also
improved, as did mobility and she was
able to walk using cross bars. Endo-
crinopathies were unaﬀected by immune-
modulation.
Discussion
This patient has PERM, which presented
as stiﬀ person syndrome (SPS) and APS
(type 1 diabetes mellitus, Hashimoto /C213s
thyroiditis, anti adrenal cortex antibodies)
with coeliac disease. Anti-GAD antibodies
are positive in 60% of cases of SPS [4].
PERM, a severe form of SPS is referred to
as an SPS /C212plus/C213disorder. SPS and SPS
/C212plus/C213disorders are associated with other
autoimmune conditions including type1
diabetes mellitus, thyroiditis, Grave /C213s
disease and myasthenia gravis.
Stiﬀ person syndrome /C212plus/C213disorders
are considered when SPS presents with
atypical features. They include PERM,
jerking stiﬀ person syndrome and stiﬀ
limb syndrome. They have poorer treat-
ment response than SPS. PERM follows a
rapid course leading to death within
3 years of onset [2]. Our patient /C213s symp-
toms of PERM have been present for
approximately 6 years. This may be the
result of immunomodulatory therapies
slowing disease progression. Oral steroids,
IV methylprednisolone, IV immunoglob-
ulin and plasma exchange during the ﬁrst
2 years of PERM were ineﬀective. Over
the subsequent 3 years, oral methotrexate,
azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil and
IV inﬂiximab were also ineﬀective. PERM
and SPS are B cell disorders [5]. This was
our basis for rituximab (anti-CD 20
monoclonal antibody) therapy. Rituximab
was commenced 3 months following inf-
liximab therapy. Within 10 days an
improvement in coordination, speech and
mobility was noted. A marked and sus-
tained improvement occurred 1 week after
cycle 2.
This case highlights an association
between two rare autoimmune conditions,
PERM and APS. PERM had a protracted
course in our patient and the necessity for
surveillance for the development of pos-
sible life-threatening autoimmune condi-
tions such as type 1 diabetes mellitus is
highlighted. Rituximab, which depletes B
cells may be an eﬀective treatment option
for PERM.
Disclosure
The authors report no conﬂicts of interest.
References
1. Lohmann T, Londei M, Hawa M, Leslie
RD. Humoral and cellular autoimmune
responses in stiﬀ person syndrome. Annals
of the New York Academy of Sciences 2003;
998: 215–222.
2. Brown P, Marsden CD. The stiﬀ man and
stiﬀ man plus syndromes. Journal of
Neurology 1999; 246: 648–652.
3. Neufeld M, Blizzard RM. Polyglandular
Autoimmune Diseases . Symposium on auto-
immune aspects of endocrine disorders. New
York: Academic Press 1980;357–365
4. Solimena M, Folli F, Aparisi R, Pozza G,
De CamilliP. Autoantibodies to GABAergic
neurons and pancreatic beta cells in stiﬀ-
man syndrome. The New England Journal of
Medicine 1990; 322: 1555–1560.
5. Raju R, Foote J, Banga JP, et al. Analysis
of GAD65 autoantibodies in stiﬀ-person
syndrome patients. Journal of Immunology
2005; 175: 7755–7762.
